# Data notes {#sec-data-notes}

*Full appendix content to be built in a later session. The notes below address cross-cutting definitions and data choices that multiple chapters reference.*

## Population series

**Two population estimates appear in this report for the same year, 2024.** The demographics chapter (@sec-demographics) leads with the U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates Program (PEP) July 1, 2024 estimate — **75,865** — because PEP is the current, point-in-time measure best suited to describing recent growth. The projections chapter (@sec-projections) bases its household-formation and forward-need estimates on the ACS 2020–2024 5-year estimate — **74,577 (Table B01003)** — because the projections model is built on ACS-derived household size (2.78, B25010) and CHAS affordability shares, which are themselves 5-year-pooled measures; using the same ACS universe keeps the inputs internally consistent. These are different measures of the same underlying population (PEP is a point-in-time July estimate; ACS 5-year is a period estimate pooling surveys from roughly 2022 in concept), and the ~1,300-person gap is expected, not a discrepancy. Readers comparing the two chapters should not assume one figure is wrong.

## ACS estimates labeled by a single year

All figures and tables in this report that cite a single calendar year for American Community Survey data (e.g., "2024") are drawn from **ACS 5-year estimates** referenced by their **end year**. The "2024" estimates pool survey responses collected from 2020 through 2024. Five-year estimates are used throughout because Fauquier County and especially its two places (Warrenton, Bealeton) have populations too small for reliable 1-year ACS estimates. Readers should not interpret a "2024" ACS figure as a point-in-time 2024 value; it reflects conditions across the full five-year survey window, with the center of the period near 2022.
